facts.summary: Connecticut's minimum wage is $16.94 per hour effective January 1, 2026, well above the federal $7.25; it adjusts annually based on the federal employment cost index.
facts.notes: $16.94 confirmed effective 1/1/2026 (up from $16.35). Indexed annually to the federal employment cost index; verify each year for the current figure.

facts.value: follows federal FLSA (1.5x after 40 hrs/week; no daily overtime; no higher salary floor)
facts.summary: Connecticut requires overtime at 1.5x the regular rate after 40 hours in a workweek, matching the federal weekly standard; there is no daily overtime requirement.
facts.notes: CT has its own overtime statute (31-76c) but the trigger is the same 40 hrs/week as federal FLSA. CT applies executive/administrative/professional duties tests; no state-specific salary threshold higher than the federal level was found on an official source.

value: status as a victim of domestic violence
facts.summary: Connecticut's Fair Employment Practices Act protects several classes beyond the federal set, including ancestry, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, veteran status, status as a victim of domestic violence, and learning/intellectual disability.
facts.sourceAgency: Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities (CHRO)
facts.notes: List captures classes ADDED beyond the federal set (race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability, genetic info, pregnancy). CT also protects those federal classes.

facts.summary: Connecticut's anti-discrimination law covers employers with three or more employees, a lower threshold than Title VII's 15.
facts.notes: 'Employer' means any person with three or more persons in employ (plus any employer of a domestic worker regardless of number). Verify subsection numbering, which may shift with amendments.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint must be filed with the CHRO within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory act.
facts.sourceAgency: Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities (CHRO)
facts.notes: Deadline extended from 180 to 300 days by P.A. 19-16 (effective 10/1/2019). Contacting CHRO or completing an inquiry form does not itself constitute filing. Verify exact subsection of 46a-82.

facts.summary: Actions to recover unpaid wages generally must be brought within two years; the DOL also limits wage-complaint investigations to the two years preceding the complaint.
facts.notes: Two-year statute of limitations under § 52-596 for remuneration for employment. Successful claimants may recover double damages plus costs and attorney's fees under § 31-72 absent employer good-faith. Verify current limitations period.

facts.summary: Connecticut law prohibits employers from disciplining or discharging an employee who reports a suspected violation of law or regulation to a public body; the employee may sue in Superior Court within 90 days after exhausting administrative remedies.
facts.sourceAgency: Connecticut General Assembly (Office of Legislative Research)
facts.notes: Private-sector whistleblower protection. 90-day window to bring civil action after exhausting administrative remedies. Separate statutes cover public employees (§ 4-61dd) and health-care workers (§ 19a-532).

facts.value: discharge: next business day; quit or layoff: next regular payday
facts.summary: A discharged employee must be paid all wages by the next business day, while an employee who quits or is laid off must be paid by the next regular payday.
facts.notes: Federal law sets no final-pay deadline, so this is a CT addition. Confirm the linked DOL PDF is the current version.
